Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research

Internal Brace Augmentation for Scapholunate Interosseous Ligament Injuries Is Supported by Limited Evidence and Is Associated With Early Failures: A Systematic Review

Roh YT, Lee JY, Im JH et al. · 2026 Oct 30
Study Type: Systematic review (PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO-registered); narrative synthesis, no meta-analysis. 11 studies (2 comparative, 9 single-arm; 161 wrists), follow-up 12–50 months.
Key Question: Does internal brace augmentation of scapholunate ligament repair or reconstruction improve outcomes, maintain carpal alignment, and avoid perianchor osteolysis and structural failure?
Key Findings:
  • Single-arm series showed improved VAS pain (6–8 to 0–4), grip strength (62% to 98% of contralateral) and scapholunate gap (4–6 mm to 2–3 mm). The two comparative studies found no pain, function or disability benefit over reconstruction or fixation without the brace.
  • Perianchor osteolysis occurred in 36–59% of patients where assessed (59% at 50 months), versus 0% in one all-arthroscopic series. One comparative study reported 36% versus 0% for RASL control.
  • The only study with follow-up beyond 4 years (n=18) reported structural failure in 44%.
Clinical Relevance: Internal brace augmentation should not be adopted routinely; patients should be counselled on late failure and osteolysis, and prospective use should include radiographic surveillance (ideally within a registry or audit).
Limitations: Evidence is predominantly low-quality single-arm data with short, incomplete follow-up, unblinded assessment and selection bias, probably overstating benefit and understating harm.

Journal of Arthroplasty

The 10-Year Revision Risk of Dual-Mobility Versus Standard Cups in Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis: A Population-Based Study from the Danish Hip Arthroplasty Register

Hussein Y, Iljazi A, Sørensen MS et al. · 2026 Oct 27
Study Type: Nationwide register-based cohort study (Danish Hip Arthroplasty Register), 2007–2019.
Key Question: Does 10-year revision risk differ between monoblock dual-mobility (DM) cups and standard cups with 32 or 36 mm heads in primary THA for osteoarthritis?
Key Findings:
  • Standardised 10-year all-cause revision risk: DM 6.6% (95% CI 5.7–7.4), SC36 5.9% (5.6–6.3), SC32 6.9% (6.4–7.4). No significant difference for DM vs SC36 (−0.6 pp, 95% CI −1.5 to 0.3) or DM vs SC32 (0.3 pp, −0.6 to 1.3).
  • DM was associated with lower revision risk for dislocation than both standard cup groups.
  • DM was associated with higher revision risk for infection than both standard cup groups (effect sizes not reported in abstract).
Clinical Relevance: In primary OA, DM cups offer no overall revision advantage at 10 years, so routine use should be weighed against a possible infection signal, though dislocation-specific benefit may still matter in higher-risk patients.
Limitations: Observational design leaves residual confounding possible, and the small DM cohort (n=5,187) limits precision for cause-specific outcomes.

The Journal of Bone & Joint Surgery

Implant Choice Impacts Initial Tibial Component Micromotion in Total Ankle Replacement: A Biomechanical Analysis

Henry JK, Hoffman J, Villar R et al. · 2026 Oct 29
Study Type: Cadaveric biomechanical study (matched-pair, n=10 pairs) using a robotic gait simulator
Key Question: Does tibial component design (stemmed vs low-profile) affect time-zero bone-implant micromotion in total ankle replacement?
Key Findings:
  • Peak micromotion was greater with low-profile implants by 150 µm (95% CI 98–203; p<0.001) versus matched stemmed implants.
  • Mean micromotion was greater with low-profile implants by 30 µm (95% CI 9–52; p<0.001).
  • Low-profile implants showed posterior peak micromotion consistent with rocking; stemmed implants showed more even distribution, with peak motion at the stem tip.
Clinical Relevance: These data offer a plausible mechanical explanation for higher early failure rates reported with low-profile tibial components, which may inform implant selection and counselling in UK TAR practice.
Limitations: Time-zero cadaveric testing in a young cohort (mean age 48) cannot capture bone quality in typical TAR patients, osseointegration, or long-term clinical outcomes, and absolute micromotion thresholds for failure were not established.

Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research

Does a Prior Unsuccessful DAIR Increase the Risk of Reinfection After a Two-stage Revision for Periprosthetic Joint Infection? Results of a Multicenter Case-control Study

Barbero Allende JM, Fernández E, Gómez-Junyent J et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Multicentre retrospective case-control study (12 Spanish hospitals, 2009–2018; 89 cases, 171 matched controls), Level III evidence.
Key Question: Does a prior unsuccessful DAIR increase the risk of reinfection after two-stage revision for PJI, compared with proceeding directly to two-stage revision?
Key Findings:
  • Prior failed DAIR was associated with higher odds of reinfection within 2 years of reimplantation (adjusted OR 3.5, 95% CI 1.4–8.8; p = 0.008).
  • Association appeared stronger in chronic PJI (aOR 4.0, 95% CI 1.4–11.3) than acute PJI (aOR 2.2, 95% CI 0.7–7.2), but the interaction test was non-significant.
Clinical Relevance: Supports careful patient selection for DAIR in UK practice, as a failed attempt may compromise subsequent two-stage outcomes, particularly in chronic infection.
Limitations: Retrospective design with a modest sample and wide confidence intervals limits causal inference and subgroup conclusions; residual confounding (e.g., DAIR timing, pathogen) is possible.

Journal of Arthroplasty

Prospective Evaluation of an Intraoperative Synovial Calprotectin Point-of-Care Lateral Flow Test for Periprosthetic Joint Infection in Hip and Knee Revisions

Giatroudakis K, Iliopoulos E, Kateros K et al. · 2026 Oct 27
Study Type: Prospective consecutive diagnostic accuracy cohort study (single-centre, n=80).
Key Question: How accurately does an intraoperative synovial calprotectin lateral flow test (≥50 mg/L) diagnose PJI in revision hip and knee arthroplasty, against 2018 ICM criteria?
Key Findings:
  • THA (n=55): sensitivity 91.7% (95% CI 73.0–99.0), specificity 90.3% (74.2–98.0), AUC 0.894.
  • TKA (n=25): sensitivity 87.5% (47.3–99.7), specificity 100% (80.5–100), AUC 0.930; only 8 PJI cases.
  • Three false positives (metallosis, recent dislocation, unexplained inflammation); three false negatives (fungal infection, culture-negative PJI with sinus tract).
Clinical Relevance: A fresh-sample, on-label rapid test could support intraoperative decisions (e.g. single- versus two-stage revision) where frozen section or rapid cultures are unavailable in NHS theatres.
Limitations: Small sample, especially TKA (wide CIs), and a single-centre design limit generalisability; the false-negative and false-positive patterns suggest the test cannot replace a full diagnostic work-up.

Journal of Arthroplasty

Porous Tantalum Acetabular Components in Complex Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty: The Influence of Defect Severity and Intraoperative Fixation

D'Apollonio TM, Oteman BPH, Hopman MLT et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Retrospective single-centre cohort study (345 hips, 2003–2024; mean follow-up 6.5 years).
Key Question: What are the re-revision rates of porous tantalum acetabular components in complex revision THA, and how do defect severity and intraoperative fixation influence them?
Key Findings:
  • Cumulative incidence of re-revision for aseptic loosening was 0.87%, 1.84% and 2.72% at 2, 5 and 10 years; all-cause acetabular re-revision was 5.52%, 7.40% and 9.23%.
  • Paprosky grade (2A–3B) and pelvic discontinuity (23.8% of hips) were not associated with re-revision risk.
  • Third or greater revision increased failure risk (sHR 2.69, P=0.03); three-point fixation was independently protective (sHR 0.37, P=0.04), whereas press-fit was not after adjustment.
Clinical Relevance: Supports porous tantalum as a reliable option for severe acetabular defects, and suggests prioritising three-point fixation intraoperatively, which is relevant to NHS revision centres managing complex bone loss.
Limitations: Retrospective design with few events limits statistical power, and the lack of association with defect grade may reflect a type II error; no comparator implant was used.

The American Journal of Sports Medicine

Association of Changes in Game Pitch Count, Pitching Velocity, and Arm Injuries in Collegiate Pitchers

Salamh P, Plisky P, Beiting J et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Prospective cohort study (Level 2 evidence)
Key Question: Are within-pitcher changes in game pitch count and fastball velocity associated with shoulder and elbow injury risk in collegiate baseball pitchers?
Key Findings:
  • 187 pitchers followed across 9,890 exposure days; 22 (12%; 95% CI 7.5–17.2%) sustained an arm injury.
  • Injury hazard showed a nonlinear (parabolic) association with deviation of pitch count from the individual pitcher's seasonal mean.
  • Injury hazard also showed a nonlinear (parabolic) association with a fall in fastball velocity relative to the pitcher's own mean. Hazard ratios were not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Individualised workload and velocity monitoring may help identify overhead athletes at risk, though the data come from US collegiate baseball and are of limited direct relevance to UK practice.
Limitations: Few injury events (n=22) in a single summer season limits precision and the ability to adjust for confounders; effect sizes are not given in the abstract.

The American Journal of Sports Medicine

The Critical-Size Osteochondral Defect for Single-Hole Microfracture Repair in Rats: A Center-Initiated, Perforation-Anchored Healing Pattern With Limited Spatial Coverage

Lu J, Yuan Y, Zhang W et al. · 2026 Oct 23
Study Type: Controlled laboratory study (preclinical, in vivo rat model). Sample size not stated in the abstract.
Key Question: What is the maximum osteochondral defect diameter that can heal from a single microfracture perforation, and how does repair spread spatially from that channel?
Key Findings:
  • At 8 weeks, 1 mm and 1.5 mm defects showed better filling, subchondral bone reconstruction and COL II expression than 2 mm defects (all P < .05), with no significant difference between 1 mm and 1.5 mm.
  • Reparative tissue (safranin O staining, COL II) concentrated around the perforation tract and declined significantly towards the defect periphery (P < .05).
  • The authors propose ~1.5 mm as the critical defect gap for single-hole microfracture.
Clinical Relevance: The findings suggest each microfracture channel has limited effective coverage, which may inform perforation spacing and density, but the findings cannot be translated directly to human defect sizes or current NHS practice.
Limitations: Small-animal model with 1 mm deep defects and 8-week follow-up; the 1.5 mm threshold cannot be extrapolated to human cartilage thickness, loading or long-term outcomes.
